cards.rueckseite:
- **Cancer:** history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, age > 50, failure to improve after 1 month, pain at rest/night
- **Infection:** fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, recent UTI/skin infection, spinal procedure
- **Fracture:** significant trauma, age > 70, steroid use, osteoporosis
- **Cauda equina:** urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral or progressive deficits
- AAA (pulsatile mass, older men)

Without red flags: no imaging in the first ~6 weeks; ≈ 90% improve within 1 month.

zeilen: Disc tissue beyond the vertebral body edges over **> 25% (> 90°)** of the circumference
Focal (< 25%), base **wider** than the displaced material in every plane
Displaced material **wider than its base** in at least one plane, or extends cranially/caudally beyond the disc level
Extruded fragment that has **lost continuity** with the parent disc (free fragment)
Displacement away from the extrusion site (cranial/caudal), with or without sequestration

cards.vorderseite: Straight leg raising and related signs
cards.rueckseite:
- **Lasègue (SLR):** pain radiating below the knee at **30–70°** of hip flexion; tests L5/S1; sensitive (≈ 83%) but not specific
- **Crossed SLR** (Fajersztajn): raising the **opposite** leg reproduces sciatica → **highly specific** (≈ 90%) for disc herniation, often axillary/central
- **Bowstring, Bragard:** confirmatory maneuvers
- **Femoral stretch (reverse SLR):** prone knee flexion/hip extension → anterior thigh pain = **L2–L4** (upper lumbar or far lateral L4–5 disc)
- **Waddell signs** (≥ 3 of 5: superficial tenderness, simulation, distraction, regional disturbance, overreaction) → nonorganic component

cards.vorderseite: Cauda equina syndrome: definition and timing
cards.rueckseite:
Requires ≥ 1 of: **bladder/bowel dysfunction**, **saddle anesthesia**, new sexual dysfunction (± leg deficits).
- **Urinary retention:** most consistent finding (sensitivity ≈ 90%) → check **post-void residual** (> 100–200 mL abnormal); overflow incontinence
- Saddle anesthesia: most common sensory deficit; anal tone reduced in 60–80%
- Causes: large central lumbar disc (usually L4–5), tumor, hematoma, abscess, stenosis
- **Urgent MRI**; decompression ideally **within 48 h** (better outcome for bladder and motor function; some argue earlier, especially before retention develops)

≈ 3–10% of lumbar herniations; in or lateral to the foramen; most common **L4–5 and L3–4**.
Compresses the **exiting root of the same level** (L4–5 → **L4**), not the traversing root.
**Clinic:** severe radicular pain, often worse in extension and lateral bending, **positive femoral stretch test**, weak quadriceps/absent knee jerk; SLR often negative.
**Imaging:** easily missed on myelography; seen on axial MRI/CT lateral to the facet.
**Surgery:** paramedian **Wiltse (muscle-splitting) intertransverse approach** or partial facetectomy; avoid destabilizing complete facetectomy.

cards.vorderseite: Upper lumbar disc herniation (L1–2 to L3–4)
cards.rueckseite:
Only ≈ 5% of lumbar disc herniations; more often in older patients and after previous lower lumbar surgery.
**Signs:** anterior thigh pain, **quadriceps weakness**, reduced **knee jerk** (L3–4), positive **femoral stretch test**; SLR usually negative.
Higher levels (L1–2) can involve the **conus** → mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs, sphincter disturbance.
Differential: hip disease, diabetic amyotrophy, femoral neuropathy, retroperitoneal hematoma.

cards.text: Lumbar discectomy risks: mortality ≈ {{c1::0.06%}}, superficial infection 0.9–5%, unintended durotomy {{c2::0.3–13% (≈ 18% in revisions)}}, recurrent herniation ≈ {{c3::4–10%}}. Rare but deadly: perforation of the anterior annulus with {{c4::aortic/iliac artery or vein injury}} (hypotension and tachycardia during or after surgery → emergency laparotomy).

cards.rueckseite:
- **Wrong diagnosis** (e.g., hip, peripheral nerve, nonorganic)
- **Wrong operation/inadequate** decompression (missed lateral recess or foraminal stenosis, wrong level, retained fragment)
- **Recurrent or new herniation**, adjacent segment degeneration
- **Instability** (iatrogenic), pseudarthrosis, hardware failure
- **Epidural fibrosis (scar)**, **arachnoiditis**
- Infection (discitis), pseudomeningocele
- Psychosocial factors, compensation

Work-up: contrast MRI, flexion–extension X-rays, CT. Treatments: rehabilitation, **spinal cord stimulation** (better than reoperation for radicular pain), revision when a correctable lesion exists.

Inflammation and fibrosis of the arachnoid with **clumping of nerve roots**.
**Causes:** previous surgery (especially multiple), **oil-based myelographic contrast (Pantopaque)**, intrathecal steroids/blood, infection, hemorrhage.
**MRI:** central clumping of roots, peripheral adhesion to the dura ("empty sac"), or a soft-tissue mass filling the sac.
Clinic: chronic burning leg and back pain, variable deficits.
Treatment: largely symptomatic (surgery usually unhelpful); SCS sometimes.

Pain at the coccyx, worse **sitting** and rising from sitting; women > men (5:1).
**Causes:** trauma (fall, childbirth), hypermobile or subluxed coccyx, idiopathic; rule out tumors (**chordoma**, sacral tumors, giant cell), infection, referred pain (pelvic disease).
**Work-up:** dynamic sitting/standing lateral X-rays, MRI if red flags.
**Treatment:** cushions (donut/wedge), NSAIDs, local injections, manipulation; **coccygectomy** for refractory cases (good results in selected patients, infection risk).

- **Spurling sign:** neck extension + rotation/lateral flexion toward the symptomatic side + axial compression reproduces radicular pain (specific, poorly sensitive)
- **Shoulder abduction relief sign:** hand placed on top of the head relieves pain (C4–C6)
- **Lhermitte sign:** electric shock down the spine on neck flexion (cord: MS, spondylosis, tumor, cervical radiation)
- Root affected is the **lower** number at a cervical level (C5–6 → C6)
- C5–6 and C6–7 most common (C7 root most often)

zeilen: Root signs and symptoms, no cord involvement
Signs of cord involvement, normal gait
Mild gait involvement, able to be employed
Able to ambulate only with assistance
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 83.2, p. 1299. mJOA (Benzel, 0–18): mild ≥ 15, moderate 12–14, severe ≤ 11; surgery recommended for moderate/severe CSM (AO Spine/WFNS).

cards.rueckseite:
- **Hoffmann sign** (flick the middle finger nail → thumb/index flexion)
- **Inverted radial reflex** (tapping brachioradialis → finger flexion without elbow flexion; C5–6 lesion)
- **Scapulohumeral reflex** (lesion above C3)
- **Myelopathy hand:** finger escape sign (ulnar fingers drift into abduction), poor grip-release (< 20 in 10 s), intrinsic wasting
- Broad-based spastic gait, Babinski, clonus, Romberg (posterior columns), Lhermitte
- Sphincter disturbance is late
Differential: ALS (no sensory loss, bulbar signs, fasciculations), B12 deficiency, MS, NPH.

- **Pelvic incidence (PI)** = **pelvic tilt (PT) + sacral slope (SS)**; PI is fixed in adults (morphologic), PT and SS change with posture
- **Lumbar lordosis** should be about **PI ± 10°** (**PI–LL mismatch** < 10° normal)
- **Sagittal vertical axis (SVA):** C7 plumb line to the posterosuperior S1 corner, normal < 4–5 cm
- **PT** < 20° normal; high PT = pelvic retroversion compensating for lost lordosis
- **Cobb angle:** between the most tilted end vertebrae; scoliosis ≥ 10°

Positive sagittal imbalance correlates best with disability (SRS-Schwab).

cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1353–1354. Coronal curve types: T (thoracic), L (thoracolumbar/lumbar), D (double), N (no coronal curve ≥ 30°).

zeilen: Complete facet resection: **Smith-Petersen / Ponte** (needs a mobile disc)
**Pedicle subtraction osteotomy** (closing wedge through the body)
Extended PSO including endplate and disc

cards.rueckseite:
Girls ≫ boys for progressive curves; usually **right thoracic**; painless (pain or **left thoracic curve** → MRI for syrinx/Chiari/tumor).
**Progression risk:** skeletal immaturity (**Risser 0–1**, premenarchal), larger curve, double curves.
- **< 20–25°:** observation
- **25–40/45°** and growth remaining: **bracing** (≈ 18 h/day; BrAIST: reduces progression to surgery)
- **> 45–50°:** posterior instrumented fusion (curves > 50° tend to progress even after maturity)
Lenke classification guides fusion levels.

zeilen: Dysplastic L5–S1 facets/sacrum; children; high risk of progression
**Pars defect** (IIA stress fracture, IIB elongated pars, IIC acute fracture); most common in young people, usually L5–S1
Facet arthrosis, intact pars; older women, **L4–5**, rarely > grade II
Acute fracture of posterior elements other than the pars
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1338–1340. Meyerding grade (slip as % of the S1 endplate): I < 25%, II 25–50%, III 50–75%, IV 75–100%, V > 100% (spondyloptosis).

cards.rueckseite:
Cysts arising from a degenerated **facet joint** (synovial lining) or ligamentum flavum (ganglion); most common at **L4–5**, often with **degenerative spondylolisthesis**.
**Clinic:** radiculopathy or stenosis symptoms, sometimes sudden (hemorrhage into the cyst).
**MRI:** cystic lesion posterolateral in the canal adjacent to the facet, rim enhancement, may contain blood/gas.
**Treatment:** percutaneous aspiration/rupture (high recurrence), **surgical excision with decompression**; consider fusion if instability.

**Risk factors:** **smoking** (strongest, ≈ 2–5×), multilevel fusion, long fusions to the sacrum, prior radiation, steroids, diabetes, osteoporosis, NSAIDs in the early postoperative period (high dose), malnutrition, inadequate graft/decortication.
**Signs:** persistent or recurrent pain, hardware loosening (halo around screws), broken rods, motion on flexion–extension films; **CT** at ≥ 6–12 months is best to assess bridging bone.
**Treatment:** revision with improved fixation, anterior column support, bone graft/BMP.

Abnormal bone remodeling (lytic → mixed → sclerotic); **lumbar spine and sacrum** most common in the spine; elevated **alkaline phosphatase**.
**Imaging:** enlarged vertebra with thickened cortex ("**picture frame**" vertebra) or "ivory vertebra".
**Neurosurgical problems:** spinal stenosis/myelopathy (bony overgrowth), compression fractures, **basilar invagination**, hearing loss, very **vascular bone** (heavy surgical bleeding → treat with bisphosphonate/calcitonin preoperatively).
**Sarcomatous degeneration** in < 1% (sudden pain increase).

Juvenile structural thoracic (or thoracolumbar) kyphosis.
**Criteria (Sorensen):** **≥ 3 adjacent vertebrae wedged ≥ 5°**; also endplate irregularity, **Schmorl nodes**, disc space narrowing; thoracic kyphosis > 45°.
Unlike postural kyphosis, it does not correct on hyperextension.
**Treatment:** observation/physical therapy; bracing in growing patients with 50–75°; surgery for > 75°, progression, pain or neurologic deficit (rarely due to thoracic disc herniation).

Ligamentous laxity (TAL) and odontoid anomalies (os odontoideum): radiographic atlantoaxial instability in ≈ 10–20%, symptomatic in 1–2%.
Screening with lateral flexion–extension X-rays is debated; ADI > 4.5–5 mm significant.
**Symptoms:** neck pain, torticollis, gait change, loss of bladder control, new myelopathic signs → MRI.
**Treatment:** asymptomatic with large ADI → avoid high-risk sports; symptomatic or ADI > 10 mm → **C1–C2 fusion** (high complication/nonunion rates). Also occipitocervical instability possible.

Excess epidural fat compressing the thecal sac, mainly **thoracic** (steroids) and **lumbar** (obesity).
**Causes:** **chronic exogenous steroids** (most common), Cushing syndrome, obesity, hypothyroidism, idiopathic.
**MRI:** T1-bright epidural fat, "**Y-sign**" (trefoil) of the compressed sac on axial lumbar images.
**Treatment:** reduce steroids, **weight loss** first; laminectomy with fat debulking for progressive deficit (higher complication rate in steroid-dependent patients).

Lumbosacral transitional vertebra (prevalence 4–8%): an **enlarged transverse process of L5 (or the last lumbar vertebra)** articulates or fuses with the **sacrum/ilium** (pseudoarthrosis).
Possible source of low back pain (controversial), accelerated **degeneration at the level above**, L5 radiculopathy at the far-out foramen.
Important for **level counting** (wrong-level surgery).
Treatment: injections, resection of the pseudoarticulation or fusion in selected cases.

Usually **anterior spinal artery** territory → **anterior cord syndrome**: sudden paraparesis/tetraparesis, loss of pain/temperature, **preserved proprioception/vibration**, sphincter loss; often with back pain.
**Causes:** **aortic surgery/aneurysm repair** (thoracoabdominal, Adamkiewicz), aortic dissection, hypotension, vasculitis, embolism (fibrocartilaginous from disc), epidural injections (particulate steroids), sickle cell.
**MRI:** "**owl eyes**"/pencil-like T2 signal in the anterior horns, DWI restriction (early MRI may be normal).
**Treatment:** supportive, raise MAP; **lumbar CSF drainage** for perioperative aortic cases.

Young **males (15–20 years)**: insidious, painless, asymmetric **wasting of C8–T1 hand/forearm muscles** (sparing brachioradialis: "oblique amyotrophy"), **no sensory loss**; progresses for a few years then stabilizes.
**Mechanism:** **forward shift of the posterior dura in neck flexion** compressing the lower cervical cord.
**MRI in flexion:** detached posterior dura with an enhancing epidural venous plexus; cord atrophy.
Differential: ALS (progressive, UMN signs).
**Treatment:** **cervical collar** to prevent flexion; anterior fusion/duraplasty in progressive cases.

Cord herniates through a **ventral (anterior) dural defect**, usually **T2–T8**, often adjacent to a calcified disc or bony erosion.
**Clinic:** slowly progressive **Brown-Séquard syndrome** (or spastic paraparesis), middle-aged women.
**MRI:** focal **ventral kinking** of the cord with an enlarged dorsal CSF space and **no** discrete dorsal cyst wall.
**Key differential:** dorsal **arachnoid cyst/web** (scalpel sign; CSF flow artifacts interrupted).
**Treatment:** reduce the cord and repair/enlarge the dural defect (patch).

Transverse band of arachnoid tissue dorsal to the **upper thoracic** cord, displacing the cord ventrally.
**MRI:** **"scalpel sign"** (dorsal indentation of the cord resembling a scalpel blade on sagittal T2), often with a **syrinx** above or below; no discrete cyst.
Clinic: myelopathy, back pain.
**Treatment:** laminectomy and **resection of the web** (good outcome, syrinx usually regresses).

zeilen: Extradural cyst **without** nerve root fibers (IA extradural arachnoid cyst, IB sacral meningocele)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1400. Tarlov cysts rarely need treatment; symptomatic ones: aspiration/fibrin glue or microsurgical imbrication.

cards.rueckseite:
Inflammatory mass at the tip of an **intrathecal catheter**, mostly with **morphine** (also hydromorphone, baclofen rarely); incidence 0.1–5%, average after ≈ 3 years (can be months).
**Clinic:** loss of analgesic effect requiring escalating doses, new radicular pain, **myelopathy/cord compression**.
**Diagnosis:** contrast MRI or CT myelogram at the catheter tip.
**Treatment:** stop infusion through the catheter/switch to saline (many regress), replace or reposition the catheter; surgical resection for neurologic deficit. Prevention: lower concentrations, tip at the lower thoracic level.

≈ 5% of all cavernous malformations; often **thoracic**, women in their 30s–40s; multiple in familial forms (check brain MRI).
**Course:** stepwise or acute deterioration from **recurrent hemorrhage** (≈ 1.5–5% per lesion-year), can mimic MS.
**MRI:** popcorn lesion with **hemosiderin rim**, best on SWI/GRE; angiographically occult.
**Treatment:** **surgical resection** for symptomatic lesions reaching the pial surface (via posterior midline/dorsal root entry zone approach); radiosurgery not established.
